transcription.tex: In 1676 Robert Hooke published an anagram: ceiiinosssttuu.
The letters rearrange to the Latin “Ut tensio, sic vis.” Hooke published the solution in 1678.
“As the extension, so the force.” The tension in an elastic string or spring is proportional to its extension, within the elastic model.
Write \(T=kx\), where \(x\) is the extension and \(k\) is the stiffness.
Let \(l\) be the natural length and \(\lambda\) the modulus of elasticity. Since \(k=\lambda/l\), Hooke’s law becomes \(T=\lambda x/l\).
When the length doubles, \(x=l\), so \(T=\lambda\). This is why the modulus of elasticity used here is measured in newtons.

In physics, Young’s modulus is the ratio of tensile stress to tensile strain, measured in pascals. It is a material property. For a uniform string of original cross-sectional area A, the modulus used here is Young’s modulus multiplied by A.

1. In A Level maths an elastic string/spring can always be assumed to be one which obeys Hooke’s law. Beyond A Level Maths (e.g. a rubber band) elastic behaviour can be observed (i.e. it returns to its original position when the deforming load is removed) but Hooke’s Law is not obeyed. Hence the ‘limit of proportionality’ can be different to the ‘elastic limit’ – you do not need to worry about these cases!

transcription.tex: A string has natural length \(l\), modulus 123 N and stretched length \(2l\). Find the tension.
The extension is \(l\), so \(T=123\,\mathrm N\).
The same string is stretched to length \(3l\). Find its tension.
The extension is \(2l\). Doubling the extension doubles the tension to 246 N.
The same string is extended by \(2l\). Find its tension.
This is the extension in the preceding question, so \(T=246\,\mathrm N\).
A spring of natural length 3 m stretches to 6 m under a force of 99 N at each end. Find its modulus.
The length doubles, so the modulus is 99 N.
A spring of modulus 40 N is compressed to \(3l/4\). Find the compressive force.
The compression is \(l/4\), giving a force of \(40/4=10\,\mathrm N\).
A 30 N force is applied to compress a string of modulus 40 N. Can you find its extension?
A string goes slack under compression. Hooke’s law for tension cannot give its displacement.

transcription.tex: Edexcel M3 · January 2003 · Q1

A particle of mass 5 kg is attached to one end of two light elastic strings. The other ends of the strings are attached to a hook on a beam. The particle hangs in equilibrium at a distance 120 cm below the hook with both strings vertical, as shown in Fig. 1. One string has natural length 100 cm and modulus of elasticity 175 N. The other string has natural length 90 cm and modulus of elasticity \(\lambda\) newtons.\par Find the value of \(\lambda\).\par [5 marks]
The first extension is \(1.20-1.00=0.20\) m, so its tension is \(T_1=175(0.20)/1.00=35\) N. [B1]
In equilibrium the upward tensions balance the weight: \(T_1+T_2=5g\). [M1]
The second extension is 0.30 m. Substitution gives \(35+\lambda(0.30)/0.90=49\). [A1]
Rearrange to obtain \(\lambda/3=49-35=14\). [M1]
Thus the modulus of the second string is \(\lambda=42\,\mathrm N\). [A1]

transcription.tex: Question 7

An elastic spring has natural length 2a and modulus of elasticity 2mg. A particle of mass m is attached to the midpoint of the spring. One end of the spring, A, is attached to the floor of a room of height 5a and the other end is attached to the ceiling of the room at a point B vertically above A. The spring is modelled as light.\par \textbf{a)} Find the distance of the particle below the ceiling when it is in equilibrium. [8 marks]\par \textbf{b)} In reality the spring may not be light. What effect will the model have had on the calculation of the distance of the particle below the ceiling? [1 mark]

\(a+x+y+a=5 a\) [B1]\par \(y=3 a-x\) [M1]\par \(\lambda=2 m g\)\par \(\left( \uparrow \right) T_{1}=T_{2}+m g\) [M1]\par \(\frac{2 m g x}{a}=\frac{2 m g \left( 3 a-x \right)}{a}+m g\) [A1]\par \(2 x=2 \left( 3 a-x \right)+a\) [M1]\par \(2 x=6 a-2 x+a\) [M1]\par \(4 x=7 a\)\par \(x=\frac{7 a}{4}\) [A1] Distance of particle from ceiling is \(a+x=a+\frac{7 a}{4}=\frac{11 a}{4}\) [A1]
\textbf{b)} If the spring is not light, then in effect the mass would increase, the extension would increase and hence the distance of the particle below the ceiling would increase. [B1]

transcription.tex: An elastic string of natural length \(2l\) and modulus of elasticity \(4mg\) is stretched between two points A and B. The points A and B are on the same horizontal level and AB =\(2l. \)A particle P is attached to the midpoint of the string and hangs in equilibrium with both parts of the string making an angle of 30\(^{\circ}\) with the line AB. Find, in terms of \(m\), the mass of the particle.
By symmetry each half has natural length \(l\) and the same tension. The horizontal projection of \(AP\) is \(l\), so \(\cos30^\circ=l/AP\) and \(AP=BP=2l/\sqrt3\).

Each extension is \(2l/\sqrt3-l\). By Hooke’s law,\par \(T=4mg(2l/\sqrt3-l)/l\)\par \(=4mg(2\sqrt3/3-1)\).\par Resolve vertically: \(2T\sin30^\circ=Mg\), hence \(T=Mg\).\par \(M=T/g=4m(2\sqrt3/3-1)\approx0.619m\).

A particle P, of mass \(m\), rests in equilibrium on a rough plane inclined at 30\(^{\circ}\) to the horizontal. The coefficient of friction between the particle and the plane is \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\). P is attached to a fixed point A on the plane by a light elastic spring with natural length \(a\) and modulus of elasticity \(3mg\). P is free to move only in a straight line below A down the line of greatest slope. Write an inequality for the length AP.
\(R=mg\cos30^\circ=\sqrt3mg/2\), so \(F_{\max}=\mu R=mg/2\). Write \(x=AP-a\). Then \(T=3mgx/a\).
At impending upward motion friction acts downhill. Resolve along the plane:\par \(T=mg\sin30^\circ+F_{\max}=mg\).\par \(3mgx/a=mg\) gives \(x=a/3\), so \(AP_{\max}=4a/3\).
Extension: express the bounds in terms of an arbitrary coefficient of friction \(\mu\).

A particle P, of mass \(m\), rests in equilibrium on a rough plane inclined at 30\(^{\circ}\) to the horizontal. The coefficient of friction between the particle and the plane is \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\). P is attached to a fixed point A on the plane by a light elastic spring with natural length \(a\) and modulus of elasticity \(3mg\). P is free to move only in a straight line below A down the line of greatest slope. Write an inequality for the length AP.
\(R=mg\cos30^\circ=\sqrt3mg/2\), so \(F_{\max}=\mu R=mg/2\). Write \(x=AP-a\). Then \(T=3mgx/a\).

At impending downward motion friction acts uphill:\par \(mg\sin30^\circ=T+F_{\max}\).\par Hence \(T=0\), \(x=0\), and \(AP_{\min}=a\). Combining both limits gives \(a\le AP\le4a/3\). A negative signed tension would represent thrust from a compressed spring.
Set \(3mgx/a=mg\sin30^\circ\pm\mu mg\cos30^\circ\) and add \(a\) to both bounds.\par \(a(7-\sqrt3\mu)/6\le AP\le a(7+\sqrt3\mu)/6\).
Question 8

A uniform rod \(P Q\), of mass 5 kg and length 3 m, has one end, \(P\), smoothly hinged to a fixed point. The other end, \(Q\), is attached to one end of a light elastic string of modulus of elasticity 30 N. The other end of the string is attached to a fixed point \(R\) which is on the same horizontal level as \(P\) with \(R P=5\) m. The system is in equilibrium and \(\angle P Q R=90^{\circ}\). Find:\par \textbf{a)} the tension in the string [5 marks]\par \textbf{b)} the natural length of the string. [3 marks]\par Problem-solving\par First take moments about \(P\).\par → Statistics and Mechanics Year 2, Chapter 4

\(P Q R=90^{\circ} \Rightarrow Q R=4\,\mathrm{~ m}\) [B1]\par \(\cos \alpha=\frac{3}{5}; \sin \alpha=\frac{4}{5}\) [B1]\par \textbf{a)} Taking moments about \(P\):\par \(5 g \times\frac{3}{2} \cos \alpha=3 T\) [M1]\par \(5 g \times\frac{3}{2} \times\frac{3}{5}=3 T\) [A1]\par \(T=\frac{3 g}{2}=14.7\)\par Tension is 14.7 N [A1]
\textbf{b)} Using Hooke's law:\par \(14.7=\frac{30 ( 4-l)}{l}\) [M1]\par \(14.7 l=120-30 l\) [A1]\par \(44.7 l=120\)\par \(l=2.68 \dots\)\par Natural length is 2.7 m (2 s.f.) [A1]
Question 9

A light elastic string AB has natural length l and modulus of elasticity 2mg. Another light elastic string CD has natural length l and modulus of elasticity 4mg. The strings are joined at their ends B and C and the end A is attached to a fixed point. A particle of mass m is hung from the end D and is at rest in equilibrium. Find the length AD. [7 marks]

\(\uparrow\)\par \(T=mg\) throughout the length. [B1]\par So, \(mg=\frac{2mgx_{1}}{l}\Rightarrow x_{1}=\frac{1}{2}l\) [M1] [A1]\par and \(mg=\frac{4mgx_{2}}{l}\Rightarrow x_{2}=\frac{1}{4}l\) [M1] [A1]\par \(\therefore\)\par \(AD=2l+x_{1}+x_{2}\) [M1]\par \(=\frac{11l}{4}\)\par The length AD is \(\frac{11l}{4}\) [A1]
Question 10

An elastic string PA has natural length 0.5 m and modulus of elasticity 9.8 N. The string PB is inextensible. The end A of the elastic string and the end B of the inextensible string are attached to two fixed points which are on the same horizontal level. The end P of each string is attached to a 2 kg particle. The particle hangs in equilibrium below AB, with PA making an angle of \(30^{\circ}\) with AB and PA perpendicular to PB. Find:\par \textbf{a)} the length of PA [7 marks]\par \textbf{b)} the length of PB [2 marks]\par \textbf{c)} the tension in PB. [2 marks]

\textbf{a)} \(\left( \nearrow \right)\) (along PA) [M1]\par \(T_{1}=2 g \cos 60^{\circ}=g=9.8\,\mathrm{N}\) [A1]\par so \(\frac{9.8 x_{1}}{0.5}=9.8\) [M1] [A1]\par \(x_{1}=0.5\) [A1]\par \(\therefore A P=0.5+0.5\) [M1]\par \(=1\,\mathrm{m}\) [A1]\par \textbf{b)} \(\frac{P B}{A P}=\tan 30^{\circ}\) [M1]\par \(P B=A P \tan 30^{\circ}=\tan 30^{\circ}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\)
\(P B\approx 0.577\,\mathrm{m}\)\par \(=0.58\,\mathrm{m} (2 \mathrm{s. f.})\) [A1]

\textbf{c)} \(\left( \nearrow \right)\) (along PB)\par \(T_{2}=2 g \cos 30^{\circ}\) [M1]\par \(= 2 g \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\)\par \(= g \sqrt{3}\,\mathrm{~N}\)\par \(\approx 17\,\mathrm{~N}\) (2 s.f.)\par The tension in PB is 17 N (2 s.f.) [A1]
Question 11

A particle of mass 2 kg is attached to one end P of a light elastic string PQ of modulus of elasticity 20 N and natural length 0.8 m. The end Q of the string is attached to a point on a rough plane which is inclined at an angle \(\alpha\) to the horizontal, where \(\tan \alpha=\frac{3}{4}\). The coefficient of friction between the particle and the plane is \(\frac{1}{2}\). The particle rests in limiting equilibrium, on the point of sliding down the plane, with PQ along a line of greatest slope. Find:\par \textbf{a)} the tension in the string [5 marks]\par \textbf{b)} the length of the string. [2 marks]

\(\tan \alpha = \frac{3}{4}\) so \(\cos \alpha = \frac{4}{5}\) and \(\sin \alpha = \frac{3}{5}\)\par Resolving perpendicular to the plane: \(R=2g\cos \alpha=\frac{8g}{5}\) [M1]\par \(\therefore\)\par \(F=\mu R=\frac{1}{2}\times\frac{8g}{5}=\frac{4g}{5}\) [A1]\par Resolving parallel to the plane: \(T+F=2g\sin \alpha\) [M1]\par \(T=2g\sin \alpha-F\)\par \(=\left( 2g\times\frac{3}{5} \right)-\frac{4g}{5}=\frac{2g}{5}\) [A1]
\(=3.92\)\par The tension in the string is 3.9 N (2 s.f.) [A1]\par \textbf{b)} \(T=\frac{\lambda x}{l}\)
Length of the string \(=0.16+0.8\)\par \(=0.96\,\mathrm{m}\) (2 s.f.) [A1]

transcription.tex: One end of a light elastic string, of natural length 0.5m and modulus of elasticity 20N, is attached to a fixed point A. The other end is attached to a particle of mass 2kg. The particle is held at a point which is 1.5m below A and released from rest. Find:\par (a) The initial acceleration of the particle\par (b) The length of the string when the particle reaches its maximum speed.
(a) The extension is \(1.5-0.5=1\,\mathrm m\). Hence \(T=20(1)/0.5=40\,\mathrm N\). Taking upwards as positive gives \(T-2g=2a\), so \(a=(40-19.6)/2=10.2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) upwards.
(b) The speed peaks at equilibrium, where \(a=0\). Thus \(T=2g=20x/0.5\), giving \(x=0.49\,\mathrm m\). Add the natural length to find the string length: \(0.5+0.49=0.99\,\mathrm m\).
Edexcel M3 · January 2013 · Question 7

A particle P of mass 1.5 kg is attached to the mid-point of a light elastic string of natural length 0.30 m and modulus of elasticity \(\lambda\) newtons. The ends of the string are attached to two fixed points A and B, where AB is horizontal and AB = 0.48 m. Initially P is held at rest at the mid-point, M, of the line AB and the tension in the string is 240 N.\par (a)  Show that \(\lambda\) = 400. \par The particle is now held at rest at the point C, where C is 0.07 m vertically below M. The particle is released from rest at C.\par (b)  Find the magnitude of the initial acceleration of P.
(a) Initially the extension is \(0.48-0.30=0.18\,\mathrm m\). Hooke’s law gives \(240=\lambda(0.18)/0.30\), so \(\lambda=400\,\mathrm N\).

(b) Each half now has length \(\sqrt{24^2+7^2}=25\) cm and extension \(25-15=10\) cm. Thus \(T=400(10)/15=800/3\,\mathrm N\).\par Resolve upwards: \(2T(7/25)-1.5g=1.5a\). Hence \(a=89.75\ldots\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\), or \(89.8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\) (3 s.f.).
Question 2

A particle of mass 0.4 kg is fixed to one end A of a light elastic spring AB, of natural length 0.8 m and modulus of elasticity 20 N. The other end B of the spring is attached to a fixed point. The particle hangs in equilibrium. It is then pulled vertically downwards through a distance 0.2 m and released from rest. Find the initial acceleration of the particle. [4 marks]

\(T=0.4 g\)\par \(T=\frac{20 x}{0.8}\)\par \(=25 x\)\par \(25 x=0.4 g\)\par \(x=\frac{2 g}{125}\) [M1]\par After further extension,\par \((\uparrow) T-0.4 g=0.4 a\)\par \(T=\frac{20 ( x+0.2)}{0.8}\)\par \(=25 x+5\) [M1]\par So, \(25 x+5-0.4 g=0.4 a\)\par \(\left( 25 \times\frac{2 g}{125} \right)+5-0.4 g=0.4 a\)
\(a=\frac{5}{0.4}\)\par \(=12.5\) [A1]\par Initial acceleration is \(12.5\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-2}.\) [A1]
Question 3

A particle P of mass 2 kg is attached to the midpoint of a light elastic string, of natural length 0.4 m and modulus of elasticity 20 N. The ends of the elastic string are attached to two fixed points A and B which are on the same horizontal level, with AB=0.6 m. The particle is held in the position shown, with AP=BP=0.5 m, and released from rest. Find the initial acceleration of the particle and state its direction. [5 marks]

\(\uparrow\)\par \(2 T\cos \theta-2 g=2 a\) [M1]\par \(\frac{4 T}{5}-g=a\) [A1]\par Using Hooke's law:\par \(T=\frac{20 \times(1.0-0.4)}{0.4}=30\) [M1] [A1]\par \(\therefore \frac{4}{5}\times 30-9.8=a\)\par \(14.2=a\)\par Initial acceleration is \(14.2\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-2}\) upwards. [A1]
Question 4

A particle of mass 2 kg is attached to one end P of a light elastic spring. The other end Q of the spring is attached to a fixed point O. The spring has natural length 1.5 m and modulus of elasticity 40 N. The particle is held at a point which is 1 m vertically above O and released from rest. Find the initial acceleration of the particle, stating its magnitude and direction. [5 marks]

\(T=\frac{40 \times0.5}{1.5}\) [M1]\par \(=\frac{40}{3}\) [A1]\par (↑) \(T-2 g=2 a\) [M1]\par So, \(\frac{40}{3}-19.6=2 a\) [A1]\par \(a=-3.13 \dots\)\par Magnitude of initial acceleration is \(3.13\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-2}\) (3 s.f.) and the direction is downwards. [A1]
Question 5

A particle of mass 1 kg is attached to one end of a light elastic spring of natural length 1.6 m and modulus of elasticity 21.5 N. The other end of the spring is attached to a fixed point O on a rough plane which is inclined to the horizontal at an angle \(\alpha\) where tan \(\alpha=\frac{5}{12}\). The coefficient of friction between the particle and the plane is \(\frac{1}{2}\). The particle is held at rest on the plane at a point which is 1.2 m from O down a line of greatest slope of the plane. The particle is released from rest and moves down the slope.\par \textbf{a)} Find its initial acceleration. [6 marks]\par \textbf{b)} Without doing any further calculation, state how your answer to part a would change if the coefficient of friction between the particle and the plane was greater than \(\frac{1}{2}\) [1 mark]

\(\tan \alpha = \frac{5}{12}\), so from the right-angled triangle:\par \(\sin \alpha = \frac{5}{13}\) and \(\cos \alpha = \frac{12}{13}\) [B1]\par By Hooke's law:\par \(T = \frac{21.5 \times 0.4}{1.6} = 5.375\,\text{ N}\) [M1]\par \(R = 1g \cos \alpha = 9.8 \times \frac{12}{13} = \frac{117.6}{13}\) [M1]\par so, \(F = 0.5 \times \frac{117.6}{13} = \frac{58.8}{13}\) [A1]\par \(1g \sin \alpha + T - F = 1a\) [M1]
Initial acceleration is \(4.62\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-2}\) (3 s.f.). [A1]
\textbf{b)} Resultant force down the plane is \(T + g \sin \alpha - \mu R = ma\), so if \(\mu\) increases, the acceleration \(a\) would decrease. [B1]
The elastic potential energy stored by a spring or taut string is the work done in stretching it from its natural length. A spring also stores energy when compressed.
At extension \(s\), Hooke’s law gives \(T=\lambda s/l\). As the extension increases from zero to \(x\), tension increases linearly from zero to \(\lambda x/l\). The mean force is \(\lambda x/(2l)\).
Multiply the mean force by the displacement: \(E=\lambda x^2/(2l)\). The square makes the energy positive for a compressed or extended spring.
Integrate the force over the extension. Here \(s\) varies and \(x\) is the final extension:\par \(E=\int_0^x T\,ds=\int_0^x(\lambda s/l)\,ds\)\par \(=[\lambda s^2/(2l)]_0^x=\lambda x^2/(2l)\).

A light elastic spring has natural length 1.2 m and modulus of elasticity 10 N. One end of the spring is attached to a fixed point. A particle of mass 2 kg is attached to the other end and hangs in equilibrium. Find the energy stored in the spring. [3 marks]

\(( \uparrow) T=2 g\)\par \(\frac{10 x}{1.2}=2 g\) [M1]\par \(x=\frac{2.4 g}{10}=0.24 g\)\par Energystored \(=\frac{10 \times(0.24 g)^{2}}{2 \times1.2}\) [M1]\par \(=23.04 \dots\)\par Energy stored in the spring is 23 J (2 s.f.) [A1]
Question 6

An elastic string has natural length a. One end is fixed. A particle of mass 2m is attached to the free end and hangs in equilibrium, with the length of the string 3a. Find the elastic potential energy stored in the string. [3 marks]
\(\frac{\lambda \times2 a}{a}=2 m g\) [M1]\par \(\Rightarrow\lambda=m g\)\par Energy stored \(=\frac{\lambda x^{2}}{2 l}\) [M1]\par \(=\frac{m g(2 a)^{2}}{2 a}\)\par \(=2 m g a\) [A1]
Question 7

A particle P of mass m is attached to one end of a light elastic string, of natural length a and modulus of elasticity 2mg. The other end of the string is attached to a fixed point O.\par The particle P is held in equilibrium by a horizontal force of magnitude \(\frac{5}{4} mg\) applied to P.\par This force acts in the vertical plane containing the string, as shown in the diagram.\par Find:\par \textbf{a)} the tension in the string [5 marks]\par \textbf{b)} the elastic energy stored in the string. [4 marks]

\(T \cos \theta=\frac{5 m g}{4}\) [M1]\par \(\uparrow\)\par \(T \sin \theta=m g\) [M1]\par So, \(\frac{T \sin \theta}{T \cos \theta}=\tan \theta=\frac{m g}{5 m g / 4}=\frac{4}{5}\) [A1]\par So, from the right-angled triangle:\par \(\sin \theta=\frac{4}{\sqrt{41}}\) and \(\cos \theta=\frac{5}{\sqrt{41}}\)\par So, \(T=\frac{m g}{\sin \theta}=\frac{m g}{4 / \sqrt{41}}=\frac{\sqrt{41} m g}{4}\) [M1]
The tension in the string is \(\frac{\sqrt{41} m g}{4}\) N [A1]

\textbf{b)} Using Hooke's law, \(T=\frac{2mgx}{a}\) [M1]\par So \(\frac{\sqrt{41}mg}{4}=\frac{2mgx}{a}\)\par and \(x=\frac{\sqrt{41}}{8}a\) [A1]\par Elastic energy stored \(=\frac{\lambda x^{2}}{2l}\) [M1]\par \(=\frac{2mg}{2a}\left(\frac{41a^{2}}{64}\right)\)\par \(=\frac{41mga}{64}\)\par The elastic energy stored is \(\frac{41mga}{64}\) J [A1]

transcription.tex: Edexcel M3 · June 2014 (R) · Q3

One end A of a light elastic string AB, of modulus of elasticity mg and natural length a, is fixed to a point on a rough plane inclined at an angle \(\theta\) to the horizontal. The other end B of the string is attached to a particle of mass m which is held at rest on the plane. The string AB lies along a line of greatest slope of the plane, with B lower than A and \(AB=a\). The coefficient of friction between the particle and the plane is \(\mu\), where \(\mu<\tan \theta\). The particle is released from rest.\par (a) Show that when the particle comes to rest it has moved a distance \(2a(\sin\theta-\mu\cos\theta)\) down the plane.\par [6 marks]\par (b) Given that there is no further motion, show that \(\mu\geq\frac{1}{3}\tan\theta.\)\par [5 marks]
(a) The normal reaction is \(R=mg\cos\theta\). [B1]
Let \(x\) be the distance moved. Work against friction is \(\mu mgx\cos\theta\). [B1]
Both end speeds are zero. The loss of gravitational potential energy equals the gain in elastic potential energy plus work against friction. [M1]
The loss is \(mgx\sin\theta\), and the elastic energy gained is \(mgx^2/(2a)\). [A1]
Hence \(\mu mgx\cos\theta=mgx\sin\theta-mgx^2/(2a)\). [A1]
Divide by \(mgx\) for \(x>0\) and rearrange: \(x=2a(\sin\theta-\mu\cos\theta)\). [A1]
(b) At this extension the tension is \(T=mgx/a=2mg(\sin\theta-\mu\cos\theta)\). [B1]
At limiting equilibrium against an upward motion, friction acts down the plane. [M1]
Staying at rest requires \(T\le mg\sin\theta+\mu mg\cos\theta\). [A1]
Substitute the tension: \(2(\sin\theta-\mu\cos\theta)\le\sin\theta+\mu\cos\theta\). [DM1]
So \(\sin\theta\le3\mu\cos\theta\), giving \(\mu\ge\tfrac13\tan\theta\). [A1]

transcription.tex: Question 3

A light elastic spring of natural length 2l has its ends attached to two points P and Q which are at the same horizontal level. The length PQ is 2l. A particle of mass m is fastened to the midpoint of the spring and is held at the midpoint of PQ. The particle is released from rest and first comes to instantaneous rest when both parts of the spring make an angle of \(60^{\circ}\) with the line PQ.\par \textbf{a)} Find the modulus of elasticity of the spring. [6 marks]\par \textbf{b)} Suggest one way in which the model could be refined to make it more realistic. [1 mark]

\textbf{a)} Conservation of energy\par P.E. loss \(=\) E.P.E. gain [M1]\par The distance fallen is \(l\tan60^\circ\) [M1]. Each spring extends by \(l/\cos60^\circ-l\) [A1]. Equating the lost gravitational energy to the elastic energy of both springs gives \(mgl\tan60^\circ=2\lambda(l/\cos60^\circ-l)^2/(2l)\) [M1].\par \(m g l \sqrt{3}=\lambda l\) [A1]\par \(m g \sqrt{3}=\lambda\)\par The modulus of elasticity of the spring is \(m g \sqrt{3}\) [A1]
\textbf{b)} Take into account the mass of the spring. [B1]
Question 4

A light elastic string, of natural length 1 m and modulus of elasticity 21.6 N, has one end attached to a fixed point O. A particle of mass 2 kg is attached to the other end. The particle is held at a point which is 3 m vertically below O and released from rest. Find:\par \textbf{a)} the speed of the particle when the string first becomes slack [5 marks]\par \textbf{b)} the distance from O when the particle first comes to rest. [3 marks]

\textbf{a)} Conservation of energy gives \(\Delta E_K+\Delta E_P=-\Delta E_{\rm elastic}\) [M1]. The released elastic energy is \(21.6(2)^2/(2\times1)=43.2\;\mathrm J\) [A1]. Hence \(\tfrac12(2)V^2+2g(2)=43.2\) [M1]. This gives \(V^2=43.2-39.2=4\) [A1] and therefore \(V=2\;\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\) [A1].\par \textbf{b)} By conservation of energy, the loss of kinetic energy equals the gain in potential energy. \(\frac{1}{2}\times m V^{2}=m g d\) [M1]\par \(2=g d\)\par \(\frac{2}{g}=d=0.20\dots\) [M1] Distance from O is \((1-d)=0.80\,\mathrm{m}\) [A1] (2 s.f.).
Question 5

A particle P is attached to one end of a light elastic string of natural length a. The other end of the string is attached to a fixed point O. When P hangs at rest in equilibrium, the distance OP is \(\frac{5 a}{3}\). The particle is now projected vertically downwards from O with speed U and first comes to instantaneous rest at a distance \(\frac{10 a}{3}\) below O. Find U in terms of a and g. [7 marks]

\(T = mg\) [B1]\par \(\frac{\lambda}{a} \times \frac{2a}{3} = mg\) [M1]\par \(\lambda = \frac{3mg}{2}\) [A1]\par K.E. loss + P.E. loss = E.P.E. gain [M1]\par \(\frac{1}{2} m U^2 + mg \frac{10a}{3} = \frac{3mg}{2} \times \frac{\left(\frac{7a}{3}\right)^2}{2a}\) [M1]\par \(\frac{U^2}{2} + \frac{10ag}{3} = \frac{3g}{4a} \times \frac{49a^2}{9}\) [A1]\par \(\frac{U^2}{2} = \frac{49ag}{12} - \frac{10ag}{3}\)
\(U^2 = \frac{9ag \times 2}{12}\)\par \(U = \sqrt{\frac{3ag}{2}}\) [A1]
Question 6

A particle P of mass 1 kg is attached to the midpoint of a light elastic string, of natural length 3 m and modulus \(\lambda\) N. The ends of the string are attached to two points A and B on the same horizontal level with \(AB=3\) m. The particle is held at the midpoint of AB and released from rest. The particle falls vertically and comes to instantaneous rest at a point which is 1 m below the midpoint of AB. Find:\par \textbf{a)} the value of \(\lambda\) [5 marks]\par \textbf{b)} the speed of P when it is 0.5 m below the initial position. [5 marks]

\(A P=\sqrt{1.5^{2}+1^{2}}=\sqrt{\frac{13}{4}}\)\par \(=\frac{\sqrt{13}}{2}\) [B1]\par \textbf{a)} P.E.loss = E.P.E.gain [M1]\par \(g \times1=\frac{2 \lambda \left( \frac{\sqrt{13}}{2}-\frac{3}{2} \right)^{2}}{2 \times1.5}\) [M1] [A1]\par \(\lambda=\frac{2 \times 3 g}{\left( \sqrt{13}-3 \right)^{2}}=160.35 \dots\)\par The value of \(\lambda\) is 160 N (2 s.f.). [A1]

\(A P=\sqrt{1.5^{2}+0.5^{2}}\)\par \(=\frac{\sqrt{10}}{2}\) [B1]\par K.E.gain+E.P.E.gain=P.E.loss [M1]\par \(\frac{1}{2} V^{2}+\frac{2 \lambda \left( \frac{\sqrt{10}}{2}-\frac{3}{2} \right)^{2}}{2 \times 1.5}=0.5 g\) [M1] [A1]\par \(V^{2}=g-\frac{\left( \sqrt{10}-3 \right)^{2}}{3} \times \lambda\)\par \(V=2.896 \dots\)\par When P is 0.5 m below the initial position its speed is \(2.9\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}\) (2 s.f.). [A1]
Question 7

A light elastic string of natural length 2 m and modulus of elasticity 117.6 N has one end attached to a fixed point O. A particle P of mass 3 kg is attached to the other end. The particle is held at O and released from rest.\par \textbf{a)} Find the distance fallen by P before it first comes to rest. [5 marks]\par \textbf{b)} Find the greatest speed of P during the fall. [4 marks]\par Problem-solving\par \(P\) will be travelling at its greatest speed when the acceleration \(=0\).

P.E. loss \(=\) E.P.E. gain [M1]\par \(3 g(2+x)=\frac{117.6}{4} x^{2}\) [A1]\par \(\frac{4 \times 3 g}{117.6}(2+x)=x^{2}\)\par \(0=x^{2}-x-2\) [A1]\par \(0=(x-2)(x+1)\) [M1]\par \(x=2\) or \(x=-1\)\par Ignore negative root.\par The distance fallen is 4 m. [A1]\par \textbf{b)} Greatest speed at equilibrium position [B1]\par \((\uparrow) T=3 g\)
\(\frac{117.6 \times e}{2}=3 g\) [M1]\par \(e=0.5\)\par E.P.E. gain + K.E. gain \(=\) P.E. loss
Question 8

A particle P of mass 2 kg is attached to one end of a light elastic string of natural length 1 m and modulus of elasticity 40 N. The other end of the string is fixed to a point O on a rough plane which is inclined at an angle \(\alpha\), where \(\tan \alpha=\frac{3}{4}\). The particle is held at O and released from rest. Given that P comes to rest after moving 2 m down the plane, find the coefficient of friction between the particle and the plane. [4 marks]

\(\tan \alpha = \frac{3}{4}\) so \(\sin \alpha = \frac{3}{5}\) and \(\cos \alpha = \frac{4}{5}\).\par \(R = 2g \cos \alpha = \frac{8g}{5}\)\par \(F = \mu R = \mu \frac{8g}{5}\) [M1]\par Work done against friction \(= \mathrm{P.E.~loss} - \mathrm{E.P.E.~gain}\) [M1]\par \(\mu \frac{8g}{5} \times 2 = 2g \times 2 \sin \alpha - \frac{40 \times 1^2}{2 \times 1}\) [A1]\par \(\mu \frac{16g}{5} = \frac{12g}{5} - 20\)
\(\mu = \frac{12g - 100}{16g}\)\par \(= 0.112\ldots\)\par The coefficient of friction is 0.11 (2 s.f.). [A1]

Two particles A and B of masses m and 2m, respectively, are connected by a light spring of natural length a and modulus of elasticity \(\lambda\). They are placed on a smooth horizontal table with AB perpendicular to the edge of the table, and A is held on the edge of the table. Initially the spring is at its natural length.\par Particle A is released. At a time t later, particle A has dropped a distance y and particle B has moved a distance x from its initial position (where \(x < a\)). Show that \(y+2x=\frac{1}{2} g t^{2}\).\par The value of \(\lambda\) is such that particle B reaches the edge of the table at a time T given by \(T=\sqrt{6 a / g}\). By considering the total energy of the system (without solving any differential equations), show that the speed of particle B at this time is \(\sqrt{2 a g / 3}\).

The first result can be obtained by writing the equation of motion for each particle separately and then adding the two equations to eliminate the unknown tension; two integrations with respect to time complete the working once the constants of integration (both zero) are evaluated. Using the result obtained, at the time T (given) with the value of x as a, y works out to also be a. As a consequence, conservation of energy has no elastic energy term at that instant, merely kinetic energy for each particle and the lost potential energy of A. Combining this equation with that obtained after the first integration in the initial result of the question gives simultaneous equations for the two speeds at that instant, and substituting for the speed of A gives a quadratic with the desired result as its repeated
